summary: Describes ways RA-Guard implementations can be evaded using IPv6 extension headers and updates RFC 6105 so those evasion vectors are eliminated. The original RA-Guard mechanism is the one from RFC 6105.

eli5.summary: A guard blocks fake notices, but tricksters hid them in extra wrapping. This fixes the guard.

questions: what are ipv6 rogue router advertisements
subtitle: How to build RA-Guard so attackers cannot slip forged IPv6 Router Advertisements past it using extension headers and fragments.

tldr.problem: Popular RA-Guard implementations, which block forged ICMPv6 Router Advertisements at layer-2 devices, can be evaded by hiding the message behind IPv6 Extension Headers or by fragmenting it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives six filtering rules: pass non-link-local sources and hop limits other than 255, parse the entire header chain, drop first fragments that lack the whole chain, and drop Router Advertisements or packets with unrecognized Next Header values.
tldr.outcome: Following the rules removes the described evasion vectors. It formally updates RFC 6105.

today: RFC 7113 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 6105; the metadata shows nothing obsoleting or updating it. Its rules are the implementation advice that complements the original RA-Guard specification.

sections.title: The RA-Guard Problem
sections.content:
RA-Guard mitigates attacks based on forged ICMPv6 Router Advertisement messages. A layer-2 device filters those messages by various criteria; the most basic is to discard them unless they arrive on a designated port. This only works if the device can reliably identify a Router Advertisement.

Some popular implementations were found to be easy to circumvent using IPv6 Extension Headers. The RFC describes the techniques and gives implementers advice to eliminate them. It notes the same tricks could also evade monitoring tools and probably enable stealth DHCPv6 attacks.
sections.eli5: A guard checks mail at a doorway and throws away fake notices from pretend bosses. It only works if the guard can recognize a fake notice.

sections.title: Evasion with Extension Headers
sections.content: There is no legitimate use for Extension Headers in Router Advertisements, but Neighbor Discovery implementations accept them by ignoring them. Some RA-Guard implementations look only at the Next Header field of the fixed IPv6 header instead of following the whole header chain. Such a device misses any Router Advertisement carrying a Hop-by-Hop Options or Destination Options header, so an attacker can walk right past it.
sections.eli5: If the guard only looks at the outside wrapper, a fake notice tucked inside a second wrapper looks harmless and gets through.

sections.title: Evasion with Fragmentation
sections.content:
A second vector works against all existing RA-Guard implementations the author found. If a forged Router Advertisement is split into at least two fragments, the layer-2 device cannot identify it. In one variant a Destination Options header precedes the message, producing two fragments. The Hdr Ext Len field sits in the first fragment, so a device seeing only the second fragment cannot tell how many bytes to skip to reach the ICMPv6 header.

With two Destination Options headers, the first fragment's Next Header is 60, so even that fragment does not reveal that an ICMPv6 message is being sent. Unless the device reassembles fragments, it cannot learn the message type.
sections.eli5: If the fake notice is torn in two and sent in separate envelopes, the guard sees only half of it each time and cannot tell what it is.

sections.title: The Six Filtering Rules
sections.content:
On ports not allowed to send Router Advertisements, an RA-Guard implementation must apply these rules.

  1. If the source address is not link-local (fe80::/10), pass the packet.
  2. If the Hop Limit is not 255, pass the packet.
  3. Parse the entire IPv6 header chain to see if it is a Router Advertisement, with no limit on bytes inspected. An implementation with such a limit must not claim compliance and must pass the packet when the limit is reached.
  4. If it is a first fragment (Fragment Offset 0) that does not contain the whole header chain, drop it and should log it as a security fault.
  5. If the packet is a Router Advertisement or has an unrecognized Next Header value, drop it and should log it. A configuration knob for unrecognized Next Header values must default to drop.
  6. Otherwise pass the packet.

Rules 1 and 2 mirror what RFC 4861 already requires of hosts, so off-link packets are not needlessly filtered. An ESP header is treated as the upper-layer protocol, so packets using ESP are passed. The logging should include a drop counter dedicated to RA-Guard drops.
sections.eli5: The guard must unwrap every layer, ignore mail that could never fool anyone anyway, and throw away anything half-hidden that it cannot fully read.

sections.title: Remaining Risks and Other Implications
sections.content:
Dropping first fragments while passing later fragments means a victim may hold buffers for fragments that never reassemble. That could cause denial of service if the victim lacks proper reassembly resource management, but it is not a new vector, since an attacker could always send datagrams with a missing fragment. Implementations that allow overlapping fragments, against RFC 5722, might still be open to Router Advertisement attacks, though most appear to comply.

The most effective mitigation is prohibiting fragmentation of Router Advertisements, as RFC 6980 specifies, but that needs implementation updates. RA-Guard covers only Router Advertisement attacks. A similar protection against rogue DHCPv6 servers can be evaded the same way, and the countermeasures are analogous.
sections.eli5: Even a good guard leaves a few small gaps, and the best fix is to stop people tearing notices in pieces in the first place.
